## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kākajātaka* (Ja 140), translated as "The Crow," is the tenth and concluding birth story of the *Asampadānavagga* (the fourteenth chapter) in the *Ekanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. According to its opening narrative framework, the Buddha delivered this teaching while residing at Jetavana with reference to a sagacious counselor, noting that the full surrounding circumstances are detailed in the *Bhaddasāla-jātaka* of the twelfth nipāta [SuttaCentral].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a crow king (*kākarājā*) in Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1877]. When the king of Bārāṇasī offered his kingdom to the Bodhisatta, the crow king returned it while entreating him to protect all living creatures [Sarkisyanz 1965]. Moved by his counsel, the king granted immunity to all living beings, established daily feedings of rice for the city's crows, and provided the Bodhisatta with royal fare [Sarkisyanz 1965; Fausböll 1877]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identified the king of Bārāṇasī as his disciple Ānanda and revealed that he himself was the crow king [Fausböll 1877].

Neither SuttaCentral nor the DharmaNexus database records any curated parallels, internal Pali text reuse, or cross-language matches for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
